Analysis by Richard Cowan 

Washington is all atwitter over Scott McClellen’s book – not with the “shocking revelation” that Bush lied, but that McClellen told the truth. Why would he do THAT? Why would he do that NOW? Maybe it was for the money, speculates a talking head who makes millions. 

Then there was this hilarious passage that really outraged the network anchors: “If anything, the national press corps was probably too deferential to the White House and to the administration in regard to the most important decision facing the nation during my years in Washington, the choice over whether to go to war in Iraq…. In this case, the ‘liberal media’ didn’t live up to its reputation. If it had, the country would have been better served.”

 

Gosh, I wish that someone had said that before. 

See 

Bush Should Have John – Comical Ali – Walters Explain The Iraq War, Then The Media Would Never Ask Any Embarrassing Questions. Doctrine Of Drug Czar Infallibility? Blame Canada, Again. 

To his publisher’s delight, McClellen even had a juicy bit about cocaine – to make an important point, of course. 

Here is how ABCNews relates it: 

“In 1999, at a hotel suite "somewhere in the Midwest," McClellan recalls hearing Bush's end of a phone conversation as the candidate dealt with the rumors about his drug use. 

Writes McClellan: "'The media won't let go of these ridiculous cocaine rumors,' I heard Bush say. 'You know, the truth is I honestly don't remember whether I tried it or not. We had some pretty wild parties back in the day, and I just don't remember.' 

"I remember thinking to myself, How can that be? How can someone simply not remember whether or not they used an illegal substance like cocaine? It didn't make a lot of sense."

 

And yet, McClellan concludes, "I think he meant what he said in that conversation about cocaine. It's the first time when I felt I was witnessing Bush convincing himself to believe something that probably was not true, and that, deep down, he knew was not true. And his reason for doing so is fairly obvious “political convenience." 

In 1946, George Orwell wrote, “We are all capable of believing things which we know to be untrue, and then, when we are finally proved wrong, impudently twisting the facts so as to show that we were right. Intellectually, it is possible to carry on this process for an indefinite time: the only check on it is that sooner or later a false belief bumps up against solid reality, usually on a battlefield.” 

Could someone read Orwell and still work for George Bush? 

See 

More Stupid Prohibitionist Tricks: Orwell Died Before Cliff Kincaid Was Born, But He Knew Him All Too Well. 

The ABCnews story then segues into "the CIA leak case involving Valerie Plame.” 

Of course, when McClellen found out that he was being lied to about that, and being used by the Administration, he was outraged, and now says that was the major impetus to write the book. 

He didn’t like being used? What town did he think he was in? 

But there is another cocaine story that the “liberal media” have been ignoring for years, and it also just happens to involve the CIA… and other things that Bush would like to forget, like the reason for choosing an Arkansas Congressman to head the DEA. See 

The Narking of America: The Bush Team for Total War, or Just to Keep the Lid On.

and 

A Great Arkansas Journalist Examines The Story that Could Bring Down Bush And The Drug War. 

and links. 

Obviously, I should have known better when I wrote the title for that last link.
After all, I had previously written: 

If The Media Cannot Report On the Well-Known CIA Role in the Iran/Contra Cocaine Business,How Can They Begin To Tell The Story of Marijuana Prohibition? Analysis by Richard Cowan 

There is a direct connection between those stories and the government’s hostility toward medical cannabis under the last two Administrations. 

In fact, there is substantial evidence that their own problems with cocaine – and their consequent vulnerability to blackmail by the narks – kept both Clinton and Bush toeing the prohibitionist party line. And as the Mena, Arkansas, story illustrates, their “problems” were not confined just to personal use. 

The American people don’t care about the “youthful indiscretions” of middle-aged politicians. But they do care – or would if they knew about it – when a seriously ill American is driven to suicide by the Administration of some little twit who can’t remember snorting coke, but can remember to cover up Mena. 

See 

The Murder of Robin Prosser. An Indictment of Karen Tandy and Motorola – By Their Own Words and Standards.

See
